extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of aesthetics, literary critics, poets and playwrights
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for composing and judging lyrical, epic, dramatic (tragedy/comedy) poetry and the value and method of history; discusses aims, effects, structure, and appropriate materials/examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ancient settings in narrative poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative poems which transfer their scene to ancient Greece or Rome lose concreteness and individualisation because our knowledge of antiquity's everyday details is insufficient and fragmentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet is obliged to avoid much and content himself with generalities, which makes the work abstract, empty, and tedious. Exception: Shakespeare avoids this by presenting, under Greek/Roman names, Englishmen of his time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyrical neglect of logical connection for unity of mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyrical poems may intentionally lack logical connection and contain gaps in thought in order that a unity of fundamental sensation and mood may predominate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This negligence makes the fundamental sensation pass like a thread through separate images, enabling quick changes of objects of contemplation (analogous to musical modulation). Examples: certain Odes of Horace, Goethe’s songs, and Petrarch’s Canzone beginning 'Mai non vo’ più cantar...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective nature of drama
rubrics_metrics.description: In drama the objective element is exclusively present: the end is to show in example the nature and existence of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama should present actions and events that make character manifest; the representation interweaves character (nature) and existence (fate/action), and may emphasize one or the other but cannot separate them in representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic as middle path between lyric and drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry is mainly objective like drama but includes a subjective element which appears in tone, delivery form, and scattered reflections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic does not entirely lose sight of the poet as in drama; it occupies a broad middle path from narrative romance to epos proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama's central goal: exhibit human nature via significant characters in situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Both drama and epic aim to exhibit, in significant characters placed in significant situations, extraordinary actions that reveal human nature and existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet most completely attains this by introducing characters in a state of peace, then allowing motives to enter and escalate through successive actions until passionate excitement reveals latent qualities of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-centred vs plot-centred pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic works range between extremes: those centring on character (principal emphasis on character) and those centring on plot (principal emphasis on action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although separable in conception, in representation character and action are entwined: circumstances and fate make character manifest, character produces actions from which events proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive motive-action structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective dramatic progression: characters first shown in peace; a motive enters producing an action; a stronger motive arises, leading to more significant action; and so on until intense excitement yields the important actions revealing character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cascade of motive→action→stronger motive→stronger action should be timed suitably to the form of the poem to maximize revelation and dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's ability to inhabit multiple characters (ventriloquism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great poets transform themselves into each person to be represented and speak out of each with equal truth and naturalness; lesser poets project themselves onto the principal person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a poet merely makes the principal character his own voice, other persons become lifeless; examples of great ventriloquism: Shakespeare and Goethe; example of projection: Byron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy evokes the sublime leading to resignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Our pleasure in tragedy belongs to the sense of the sublime—the highest grade—which lifts us above the will and its interests and summons a turning away of the will to live (resignation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy presents the terrible side of life (chance, error, fall of the just, triumph of the wicked). Fear and sympathy are means; the ultimate effect is an awakening of consciousness that life cannot give true pleasure and thus demands renunciation or knowledge of another kind of existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic catastrophe implies awareness of another existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy demands an entirely different kind of existence—knowledge of which can only be given indirectly—so that the tragic catastrophe intensifies conviction that life is a bad dream to be awakened from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to music and colour: just as a chord or colour implies its opposite, tragedy’s presentation of the world demands the notion of an existence that does not will life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancient vs modern tragic spirit (resignation vs submission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient tragic heroes commonly show submission to fate and the gods rather than the Christian-style surrender of the will to live (resignation); modern tragedy more often attains the latter and so stands higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Œdipus Colonus, Iphigenia at Aulis, Cassandra, Hercules, Hippolytus—often show endurance or consolation in revenge rather than full renunciation. Modern examples (Shakespeare, Goethe) more fully express resignation and inner change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of time/place only matters insofar as unity of action is preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect of unity of time and place is only a fault when it destroys the unity of the action; unity of action is the essential requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict French unity (single continuous action without breadth) can make drama like a geometrical line; Shakespeare’s broader approach allows scenes and speeches that do not advance action but deepen character and circumstances, which can enrich understanding of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic poet should be inexorable and mirror human variety
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic (or epic) poet ought to know that he is fate and therefore be inexorable; he should be the mirror of the human race and represent many bad, profligate, foolish, and eccentric persons, with good or magnanimous men as rare exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This variety reflects reality; exaggerating magnanimity (as in some plays) is a fault. Examples: Homer lacks truly magnanimous characters; Iffland and Kotzebue have many magnanimous characters (criticised); Goldoni follows recommended variety well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of social rank for tragic heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons of high rank (royalty, the great and powerful) are generally best adapted for tragedy because their misfortunes have sufficient magnitude to appear terrible and are less amenable to help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic or peasant tragedy is not unconditionally rejected, but the fall from greatness has greater tragic impact ('the fall is greatest from a height'); spectators of higher rank may not be tragically affected by trivial misfortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as incitement to continued assertion of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy opposes tragedy: it incites the continued assertion of the will by presenting suffering as passing and resolving into joy, success, and amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy should highlight life’s burlesque, naïve utterances, and deviations from beauty to keep spectators in good humour; it must generally close at the moment of joy so as not to reveal what follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry superior to history for knowledge of mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: More is achieved for our knowledge of mankind by poetry than by history, because poetry deals with the universal and essential (Ideas) while history deals with the contingent particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle concurs. Poetry (art) works with the Idea; science works with concept; history cannot attain the same systematic, general explanatory power as sciences or poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: History is not a science due to lack of objective general concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: History cannot be a science because it presents co‑ordination of innumerable particulars rather than subordination under objective general conceptions; it speaks of individuals, not species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sciences can determine particulars from general concepts (e.g., laws of triangles, mammalian anatomy); history’s ‘general’ (periods, revolutions) is subjective and does not allow reliable prediction of particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'general' in history is subjective and superficial
rubrics_metrics.description: What passes for the general in history is merely a subjective generality due to inadequate individual knowledge, not an objective conception in which particulars are already thought together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even the most general historical categories (periods, governments) remain particulars (long periods, events) rather than true conceptual generals; hence historical generality is superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical detail is interesting but less reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: History becomes more interesting the more special it is, but correspondingly less trustworthy; detailed particulars are uncertain and may verge on romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of chance, concealed intentions, and complexity of motives, accurate reconstruction of particulars is difficult; sometimes understanding requires long retrospection.

rubrics_metrics.name: True value of history: rational consciousness of the human race
rubrics_metrics.description: History’s proper value lies in being the rational, reflected consciousness of the human race—what reason is to the individual, history is to the race—enabling a nation to know itself and connect present with past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History restores unity to the race’s consciousness, allows anticipation of the future, and fills gaps in collective memory; written and stone monuments are means by which the race’s unity of consciousness is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monuments and writing as preservation of collective consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Written records and durable monuments serve to restore unity to the consciousness of humanity; they are meant to speak to descendants and establish continuity across generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Destruction or disfiguration of monuments for utilitarian ends is shameful. Writing (and printing) increases the reach of history; stone monuments predate writing and aimed at lasting communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy of history should seek the unchanging (Ideas), not teleological construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A true philosophy of history should fix attention on what always is (the Ideas) rather than attempting to construe history as a planned, organic whole with a teleological end (the Hegelian project).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive, optimistic histories that posit inevitable progress to earthly perfection reflect crude realism and mythology; the proper philosophical stance recognises repetition and identity in human nature—'Eadem, sed aliter.'
